title: The Dark Expanse · Heads That Would Not Stay Dead
dek: A fight among moving giants leaves heads still alive on the ground. Oscar’s rough experiment reveals how the creatures can reform, while the failing rift gives the company little time to respond.

facts.Recorded dates: Source posts · 7 August 2026 · in-world date unresolved
facts.People: Oscar Ramon; Pappy; Scribonia; Pelegia / Pin; Djöhandrai; Kar’nak
facts.Outcome: Immediate attackers defeated; heads linked to reformation. Scribonia proposes destroying the gathered heads and Pappy assists; complete disposal is not separately confirmed. The narrator assumes everyone leaves before closure.

body:
The tear can be seen across Fenumion. Beyond it lie black stone, drifting mist and giant figures that do not all stay still. The adventurers win the fight they can see, then discover that cutting a creature down may leave the means of its return on the ground beside them.

Another scar in the sky

The opening recorded on 7, Month of Moirah, Year 3 is immense. Some witnesses say it is widening; others think they see movement inside. Those reports add to the fear without settling what the company will find. Oscar stares at the tear while more experienced travelers begin moving toward it.

Pappy leaves meditation beneath the Central Tree and gathers his things. He feels in control of the rage he is bringing into the fight. Pelegia, called Pin in the scene, flies in to help and sends a shadow spirit ahead. Scribonia sees another interruption he must answer and resolves again that he ought to find the rifts’ origin.

Oscar follows, hoping for the best and adding lightning to his sword. Djöhandrai hurries in with his blade ready, and Kar’nak arrives from Gael at the last moment. They have answered the same emergency without having assembled an expedition under one settled plan.

Black stone and pale mist

Crossing the threshold removes the familiar sky. There is no bright transition to soften it: black stone extends through streams of pale mist, under a darkness without sun, moon or stars. Ahead are giant figures. For a moment they are still; then some begin moving.

Pappy advances into the attack, surrounded by shapes resembling druidic spirits with mushroom caps like his own. A creature spreads darkness and sends eldritch force toward the company. Scribonia feels the intrusion in his body and answers with an effort of inner light. Pelegia is blinded and tries to protect himself while finding a way through the obscurity.

Scribonia calls down meteors onto the figures. Some fall. The narrator then distinguishes those that moved from others that were only marble statues. An imposing shape in the mist was not enough to tell the company which figures were living threats. Oscar, repeatedly knocked prone, watches the older adventurer’s enormous power from much closer to the ground than he would like.

The fight among the figures

The headless creature reaches for Pappy’s neck. He resists the strike and laughs back at it, though it came close. Another opponent, crowded with hands, keeps attacking; the darker creature turns its eldritch force specifically on Scribonia. The danger is not one uniform kind of animated stone.

Oscar gets to his feet and charges the headless attacker, cutting into it at close range. Djöhandrai and the companion beside him coordinate another strike through stone and flesh. As the last threats come down, Pappy calls out his praise. The scattered arrivals have given one another the help needed to finish the fight.

Afterward Pappy introduces himself. Oscar gives his name as Oscar Ramon and ruefully identifies himself as the one who spent so much of the fight prone. Pappy recognizes him from Cala’s games and treats his persistence as something worth praising. The exchange gives Oscar room to be embarrassed without dismissing what he did.

Scribonia examines the fallen dark creature and notices a rune he thinks means blood. He associates it with the corruption he experienced, then purges what he calls a curse from himself. His interpretation remains local to this encounter. It does not explain the origin of every figure or every rift.

Something left moving after the kill

When Oscar’s enemy falls, a head drops from its bag and moves briefly on the ground. The detail interrupts a clean ending to the kill. A body may be down while something it carried is still active.

Oscar starts experimenting with the remains. He cuts an opening into the body at the neck and moves the head toward it. What begins as a rough, irreverent treatment of a fallen enemy becomes dangerous when something emerges from the head and tries to attach itself to the body.

The narrator makes the movement available to those watching closely. It is not simply Oscar imagining that a dead thing might return. The company now has evidence that the remains themselves require attention before anyone can safely treat the fight as over.

A head trying to return

The rift is becoming unstable while they examine the head. Oscar responds to the attempted attachment by kicking it away from the body. Separation buys distance, but does not make the thing harmless. More tentacles emerge from it.

Further investigation connects the heads to the creatures’ ability to reform. The discovery changes the task after the battle: the company must deal with what can restore an enemy, rather than only with the body it has already brought down.

The information is specific. These heads can enable these creatures to reform. The scene does not establish that every stone figure shares the same nature, that every severed head in another realm works this way, or that the whole expanse has been cleared. Meanwhile, the unstable opening is setting a limit on how long the survivors can remain to test their understanding.

A plan before the exit closes

Scribonia asks the others to gather the heads into one place so he can destroy them together. Pappy offers help. The posts record the instruction, the intended casting and the assistance; they do not provide a separate narrator confirmation that every head is destroyed. A proposed solution cannot become a more complete ending than the surviving scene supplies.

Oscar is ready to go home and sleep. Pappy thanks him for the fight and says goodnight. Djöhandrai heads toward the opening, and Pelegia leaves with a wave. The narrator closes the encounter on the assumption that everyone has left in time.

That closing ruling matters. The expedition does not end by secretly stranding a named companion in the expanse. It also does not finish every piece of the investigation the travelers wanted to conduct. They leave with a discovery, a disposal plan and the need to get out before the boundary fails.

What the expedition learns

The black-stone expanse remains unnamed. The company has learned to distinguish inert statues from attackers, to watch the remains after a kill and to recognize a head’s role in restoring a body. Those practical findings are more certain than any complete account of the place’s origin.

The encounter also leaves a smaller piece of fellowship: Oscar’s awkward persistence is noticed by an older fighter who does not mistake repeated falls for worthlessness. In a space designed to unsettle the travelers, recognition survives beside the investigation. Continue with the other recorded rift histories →
